title: Intelligence + Continual Learning = Expertise — Yu Su, NeoCognition

primary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 96%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on continual learning as the bridge from intelligence to expertise, covering parametric/nonparametric learning, reliability vs. plasticity, and adaptation after pretraining.

summary: Yu Su opens by asking why coding agents succeed while other agents remain brittle and token-inefficient. He traces agent history from expert systems through deep RL to multimodal LLMs, which encode multi-sensory inputs into unified representations conducive to symbolic reasoning. Coding became the first mass market because code is language-native, symbolic, and structured with tests as built-in rewards. Outside coding, a modern Moravec's paradox emerges: AI excels at symbolic reasoning yet struggles with everyday digital work, which spans millions of idiosyncratic micro worlds, each with unique local physics, too heterogeneous for any monolithic static model. Su draws a sharp line between intelligence—reasoning through unfamiliar problems from context with independent episodes—and expertise—accumulated, situated competence involving reliable, efficient, judgment-based action. Experts see differently through pattern recognition, deep structure, conditionality, and judgment about when to stop. Intelligence expands search via brute-force parallelism; expertise compresses search via learned shortcuts. Continual learning bridges the two, defined as adaptive compression of experience into reusable structures with four elements: what experience to capture, how to compress it, adaptivity over time, and what reusable structures to produce. Su's key figure plots raw intelligence against expertise, finding them orthogonal; scaling intelligence alone yields the world's smartest novice. With sufficient continual learning past an intelligence threshold, expertise grows unboundedly without stronger intelligence—escaping intelligence. Su closes with implications and open questions: whether we still need ever-larger models or better continual learning algorithms; how to define and measure expertise per environment; how to reconcile reliability against plasticity (humans as existence proof); how to synergize parametric and nonparametric learning; and how specialization can generate the next internet-scale data opportunity through private-world agents learning in situ and channeling knowledge back to general models. His call to action: scale expertise as a new dimension, since intelligence is becoming abundant but expertise remains scarce. Abundant expertise would give everyone personal healthcare, financial advisors, and tutors, enable every company to build human-AI learning loops as institutional memory, and unlock new types of work currently uneconomical due to high friction.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and motivation
sections.summary: Yu Su introduces himself as Ohio State professor and NeoCognition COO, framing the talk as a conceptual distinction between intelligence and expertise to answer why coding agents succeed but other agents are token-inefficient and brittle.

sections.title: Agent history and the multimodal LLM breakthrough
sections.summary: Traces agents from expert systems through deep RL to multimodal LLMs, which for the first time encode multi-sensory inputs into unified neural representations conducive to symbolic reasoning, entering a new evolutionary stage of machine intelligence.

sections.title: Coding as the ideal first market
sections.summary: Coding agents found their first mass market because code is language-native, symbolic, structured, with tests as built-in rewards. Anthropic's revenue grew 400x in under two years driven largely by coding.

sections.title: Leaving the privileged world of code and modern Moravec's paradox
sections.summary: Outside coding, agents are brittle in enterprise and personal settings. Su frames this as a modern Moravec's paradox: symbolic reasoning is easy for AI while everyday digital work is hard, requiring different cognitive competencies.

sections.title: Millions of micro worlds with local physics
sections.summary: Modern digital society consists of millions of idiosyncratic micro worlds, each with unique local physics—structures, constraints, affordances, dynamics—too heterogeneous and dynamic for any monolithic static model. Agents must continually learn on the job.

sections.title: Defining intelligence and expertise
sections.summary: Intelligence is reasoning through unfamiliar problems from available context with independent episodes. Expertise is accumulated, situated competence: reliable, efficient, judgment-based action in a particular domain. Experts see differently through pattern recognition and deep structure.

sections.title: Expert judgment, conditionality, and world models
sections.summary: Experts understand conditionality, possess judgment and taste about quality and when to stop, and effectively build a world model of their micro world as the basis for perception, reasoning, and decision-making.

sections.title: Expanding search vs. compressing search
sections.summary: Intelligence expands search by brute-forcing many parallel attempts. Expertise compresses search by bringing the right context and applying learned shortcuts. Continual learning is the bridge from intelligence to expertise.

sections.title: Defining continual learning
sections.summary: Continual learning is adaptive compression of experience into reusable structures for future behavior, with four elements: what experience, how to compress, adaptivity, and what reusable structures for what purposes.

sections.title: Intelligence vs. expertise orthogonality and escape intelligence
sections.summary: Su's key figure plots raw intelligence against expertise, finding them orthogonal. Scaling intelligence alone yields the world's smartest novice. With strong continual learning past an intelligence threshold, one achieves unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence, escaping intelligence.

sections.title: Open questions and scaling expertise as the new frontier
sections.summary: Su poses open questions: whether ever-larger models are still needed or better continual learning algorithms suffice; how to define and measure expertise per environment; how to reconcile reliability against plasticity (humans as existence proof); how to synergize parametric and nonparametric learning; and how specialization in private micro worlds can generate the next internet-scale data opportunity via in-situ learning channeled back to general models. He calls for scaling expertise as a new dimension since intelligence is becoming abundant but expertise remains scarce, envisioning personal expert advisors for all, company-level human-AI learning loops as institutional memory, and unlocking new types of work currently uneconomical due to high friction.

demonstrations: Scheduling a meeting as constraint optimization over authority, priority, and urgency rather than simple calendar slot matching
Expert reading a bug report and immediately locating plausible failure points
Humans as existence proof of combining plasticity with dependability
limitations: Agents are extremely token-inefficient, prompting companies to curb token usage
Agents remain brittle and make silly errors in enterprise and personal settings
Computer use and continual learning difficulties persist largely unchanged
Reliability and plasticity are inherently conflicting goals in continual learning systems
Public data for training LLMs has been exhausted, requiring new data sources
quantitativeClaims: Anthropic's revenue grew 400 times in under 2 years to 40 billion annualized run rate, later cited as possibly 60 billion
Revenue growth largely driven by coding and coding-related productivity
